local M = {}

local tunnels = {}

local function normalize_platform(os_name, arch)
    if os_name ~= "Linux" then
        return nil, "unsupported operating system: " .. os_name
    end

    local arch_map = {
        x86_64 = "x86_64",
        amd64 = "x86_64",

        aarch64 = "aarch64",
        arm64 = "aarch64",
    }

    local normalized_arch = arch_map[arch]

    if not normalized_arch then
        return nil, "unsupported architecture: " .. arch
    end

    return "linux-" .. normalized_arch
end

local function asset_name(platform)
    return "nvremote-nvim-" .. platform .. ".tar.gz"
end

local function asset_url(tag, asset)
    return string.format("https://github.com/juniorsundar/neovim/releases/download/%s/%s", tag, asset)
end

local function download(url, path, callback)
    vim.fn.mkdir(vim.fs.dirname(path), "p")

    vim.system({
        "curl",
        "-fL",
        "--output",
        path,
        url,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(nil, result.stderr or "download failed")
                return
            end

            callback(path, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function upload(host, local_path, remote_path, callback)
    vim.system({
        "scp",
        local_path,
        host .. ":" .. remote_path,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "upload failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function verify_sha256(archive_path, checksum_path, callback)
    vim.system({
        "sha256sum",
        "-c",
        checksum_path,
    }, {
        text = true,
        cwd = vim.fs.dirname(archive_path),
    }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or result.stdout or "checksum verification failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, result.stdout)
        end)
    end)
end

local function install_remote(host, asset, callback)
    local archive = "~/.cache/nvremote/downloads/" .. asset
    local install_dir = "~/.cache/nvremote/install/current"

    local command =
        string.format("rm -rf %s && mkdir -p %s && tar -xzf %s -C %s", install_dir, install_dir, archive, install_dir)

    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        command,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "remote install failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, install_dir)
        end)
    end)
end

local function start_remote_server(host, callback)
    local command = [[
SOCKET="$HOME/.cache/nvremote/run/nvim.sock"
NVIM="$HOME/.cache/nvremote/install/current/bin/nvim"

mkdir -p "$HOME/.cache/nvremote/run"

if [ -S "$SOCKET" ] && "$NVIM" --server "$SOCKET" --remote-expr '1' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    exit 0
fi

rm -f "$SOCKET"

nohup "$NVIM" \
  --headless \
  --listen "$SOCKET" \
  >"$HOME/.cache/nvremote/run/nvim.log" \
  2>&1 </dev/null &

sleep 1

test -S "$SOCKET"
]]

    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        command,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "failed to start remote Neovim")
                return
            end

            callback(true, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function start_tunnel(host, remote_home, callback)
    local existing = tunnels[host]

    if existing then
        existing.process:kill(15)
        tunnels[host] = nil
    end

    local local_socket = vim.fs.joinpath(
        vim.fn.stdpath("cache"),
        "nvremote",
        "run",
        "nvim.sock"
    )

    vim.fn.mkdir(vim.fs.dirname(local_socket), "p")
    vim.fn.delete(local_socket)

    local remote_socket =
        remote_home .. "/.cache/nvremote/run/nvim.sock"

    local process = vim.system({
        "ssh",
        "-N",
        "-o",
        "ExitOnForwardFailure=yes",
        "-L",
        local_socket .. ":" .. remote_socket,
        host,
    })

    vim.defer_fn(function()
        if vim.uv.fs_stat(local_socket) then
            tunnels[host] = {
                process = process,
                socket = local_socket,
            }

            callback(true, tunnels[host])
        else
            process:kill(15)
            callback(false, "SSH tunnel did not create local socket")
        end
    end, 1000)
end

local function connect_rpc(socket)
    local channel = vim.fn.sockconnect("pipe", socket, { rpc = true })

    if channel <= 0 then
        return nil, "failed to connect to remote Neovim RPC"
    end

    return channel, nil
end

local function remote_installed(host, callback)
    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        "test -x ~/.cache/nvremote/install/current/bin/nvim",
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            callback(result.code == 0)
        end)
    end)
end

local function connect_remote(host, remote_home)
    start_remote_server(host, function(started, start_err)
        if not started then
            vim.notify(start_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
            return
        end

        start_tunnel(host, remote_home, function(ok, tunnel)
            if not ok then
                vim.notify(tunnel, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            local channel, rpc_err = connect_rpc(tunnel.socket)

            if not channel then
                vim.notify(rpc_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            local version = vim.rpcrequest(
                channel,
                "nvim_exec_lua",
                [[
                    local v = vim.version()
                    return string.format(
                        "%d.%d.%d%s",
                        v.major,
                        v.minor,
                        v.patch,
                        v.prerelease and "-dev" or ""
                    )
                ]],
                {}
            )

            vim.notify("remote Neovim: " .. version)
        end)
    end)
end

function M.probe(host)
    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        [[printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n' "$(uname -s)" "$(uname -m)" "$HOME"]],
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                vim.notify(result.stderr or "ssh probe failed", vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            local lines = vim.split(vim.trim(result.stdout), "\n")
            local remote_home = lines[3]

            local platform, err = normalize_platform(lines[1], lines[2])

            if not platform then
                vim.notify(err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            remote_installed(host, function(installed)
                if installed then
                    connect_remote(host, remote_home)
                    return
                end

                local asset = asset_name(platform)
                local url = asset_url("nvremote-test-3", asset)
                local cache_dir = vim.fs.joinpath(vim.fn.stdpath "cache", "nvremote", "downloads")
                local path = vim.fs.joinpath(cache_dir, asset)

                download(url, path, function(downloaded, download_err)
                    if not downloaded then
                        vim.notify(download_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                        return
                    end

                    local checksum_asset = asset .. ".sha256"
                    local checksum_url = asset_url("nvremote-test-3", checksum_asset)
                    local checksum_path = vim.fs.joinpath(cache_dir, checksum_asset)

                    download(checksum_url, checksum_path, function(_, checksum_err)
                        if checksum_err then
                            vim.notify(checksum_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                            return
                        end

                        verify_sha256(path, checksum_path, function(ok, verify_result)
                            if not ok then
                                vim.notify(verify_result, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                                return
                            end

                            local remote_dir = "~/.cache/nvremote/downloads"
                            local remote_path = remote_dir .. "/" .. asset

                            vim.system({
                                "ssh",
                                host,
                                "mkdir -p " .. remote_dir,
                            }, { text = true }, function(mkdir_result)
                                vim.schedule(function()
                                    if mkdir_result.code ~= 0 then
                                        vim.notify(mkdir_result.stderr or "remote mkdir failed", vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                                        return
                                    end

                                    upload(host, path, remote_path, function(ok, upload_err)
                                        if not ok then
                                            vim.notify(upload_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                                            return
                                        end

                                        install_remote(host, asset, function(ok, install_result)
                                            if not ok then
                                                vim.notify(install_result, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                                                return
                                            end

                                            connect_remote(host, remote_home)
                                        end)
                                    end)
                                end)
                            end)
                        end)
                    end)
                end)
            end)
        end)
    end)
end

function M.setup()
    vim.api.nvim_create_user_command("NvRemote", function(opts)
        M.probe(opts.args)
    end, {
        nargs = 1,
        complete = "file",
    })
end

return M

    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

      - name: Build and package portable Neovim
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            -v "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE:/work" \
            -w /work \
            alpine:3.22 \
            sh -c '
              set -eu

              apk add --no-cache \
                build-base \
                cmake \
                coreutils \
                curl \
                gettext-tiny-dev \
                git \
                linux-headers

              make CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

              ./packaging/nvremote/package-linux-x86_64.sh

              ls -lh dist/nvremote-nvim-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
            '

      - name: Smoke test portable bundle on Ubuntu
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          rm -rf /tmp/nvremote-smoke
          mkdir -p /tmp/nvremote-smoke

          tar \
            -xzf dist/nvremote-nvim-linux-x86_64.tar.gz \
            -C /tmp/nvremote-smoke

          /tmp/nvremote-smoke/bin/nvim \
            --clean \
            --headless \
            '+lua vim.treesitter.language.add("lua"); print(vim.env.VIMRUNTIME); print("TREE-SITTER OK")' \
            +qa

      - name: Upload portable Neovim bundle
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: nvremote-nvim-linux-x86_64
          path: |
            dist/nvremote-nvim-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
            dist/nvremote-nvim-linux-x86_64.tar.gz.sha256

              ./packaging/nvremote/package-linux-aarch64.sh

          mkdir -p /tmp/nvremote-smoke

          tar \
            -xzf dist/nvremote-nvim-linux-aarch64.tar.gz \

I think that's the right move — and honestly it fixes several problems at once. Here's my honest assessment:

## Why it's better than the fork approach

**What the fork costs you today:** you have to keep `juniorsundar/neovim` synced with upstream, your tags live in a fork's release page mixed with neovim's own release machinery, and your plugin hard-codes a tag (`nvremote-test-3`) — meaning every new build requires you to bump the plugin. A standalone builds-repo breaks all three:

1. **No sync burden** — the repo only contains workflows, not neovim's source. The cron job clones whatever upstream tag it finds.
2. **Predictable "latest" semantics** — GitHub gives you `releases/latest` for free on a non-prerelease. The plugin can then do `GET /releases/latest` → read `tag_name` → construct asset URLs. No hard-coded tags ever again, and you get real update checks for free ("installed 0.11.3, latest is 0.11.4 → offer upgrade").
3. **The plugin becomes a real client** — download, verify sha256, install, update, all driven by the API. That's the vscode-server architecture properly: vscode doesn't ship with node bundled at a fixed version, it resolves and downloads at runtime.

## Proposed architecture

```
┌─ cron (e.g. hourly) ──────────────────────────────┐
│ check job: GH API → latest neovim release tag      │
│ compare against this repo's latest release         │
│ if different → trigger build workflow with tag     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ↓ workflow_dispatch (tag input)
┌─ build matrix ────────────────────────────────────┐
│ linux-x86_64 (alpine container, native)            │
│ linux-aarch64 (arm runner, alpine container)       │
│ ... other archs ...                                │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          ↓
   gh release create v0.11.4 (mirror the upstream tag)
```

Key detail: make the check job tiny (no checkout, just API calls) and have it *dispatch* the heavy build workflow with the tag as an input. That way you can also run the build manually with any historical tag to backfill versions.

## Caveats worth knowing

- **GH cron isn't punctual** — it can be delayed 10–30+ minutes. Irrelevant for this use case; hourly is fine.
- **"Most archs" has a cost gradient:** x86_64 and aarch64 are native runners (fast, ~10 min builds). armv7 needs emulation via QEMU/binfmt inside the container (~30–60 min builds, occasionally flaky). Windows/macOS portable bundles are a genuinely different packaging problem (dylib path fixing, app bundles) — and your plugin currently only supports Linux anyway.
- **Tag mirroring** — naming your releases exactly `v0.11.4` etc. keeps the plugin's version logic trivial (upstream tag == your tag == installed version).

# outpost-builds

Portable, single-directory Neovim bundles for [outpost.nvim](../../dotfiles) —
built automatically whenever upstream [neovim/neovim](https://github.com/neovim/neovim)
publishes a new stable release.

Each release mirrors the upstream tag (`v0.11.4`, …) and ships musl-bundled
archives that run on any Linux with zero dependencies — no glibc version
requirements, no `libgcc` hunting. This is what lets outpost.nvim drop a
working Neovim onto any remote host over SSH.

## How it works

- **`.github/workflows/check.yml`** — runs hourly via cron. Compares the latest
  stable neovim release tag against this repo's latest release. If upstream is
  newer, it dispatches the build workflow with the tag.
- **`.github/workflows/build.yml`** — builds a matrix of targets in an Alpine
  container (so the resulting binary links against musl, not the runner's
  glibc), bundles the musl dynamic loader + runtime deps into the archive,
  smoke-tests the bundle on the Ubuntu runner, and publishes a GitHub release
  mirroring the upstream tag. Can also be dispatched manually with any
  historical tag to backfill a version.

## Assets

| Asset | Runner |
| --- | --- |
| `nvim-portable-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` | `ubuntu-24.04` (native) |
| `nvim-portable-linux-aarch64.tar.gz` | `ubuntu-24.04-arm` (native) |

Each archive is accompanied by a `.sha256` checksum.

Consumers (like outpost.nvim) can resolve the latest build with:

```
GET https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/outpost-builds/releases/latest
```

and construct download URLs as:

```
https://github.com/<owner>/outpost-builds/releases/download/<tag>/<asset>
```

## Usage

Extract anywhere and run — the bundled launcher sets up its own loader path:

```sh
tar -xzf nvim-portable-linux-x86_64.tar.gz -C nvim
./nvim/bin/nvim --headless +qa && echo OK
```

#!/bin/sh
# Package a musl-bundled, single-directory portable Neovim for the given musl arch.
#
# Usage: package.sh <x86_64|aarch64>
#
# Environment:
#   SRC_DIR  - directory containing the neovim checkout with a completed ./build (default: neovim-src)
#   DIST_DIR - output directory (default: dist)

set -eu

ARCH=${1:?usage: package.sh <x86_64|aarch64>}

SRC_DIR=${SRC_DIR:-neovim-src}
DIST_DIR=${DIST_DIR:-dist}
MUSL_LOADER="ld-musl-$ARCH.so.1"

STAGE="$DIST_DIR/stage/nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH"
ARCHIVE="$DIST_DIR/nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH.tar.gz"

rm -rf "$STAGE"
mkdir -p "$STAGE/lib"

# Install Neovim + matching runtime.
cmake --install "$SRC_DIR/build" --prefix "$STAGE"

# Preserve the real Neovim executable.
mv "$STAGE/bin/nvim" "$STAGE/bin/nvim.real"

# Bundle the musl runtime dependencies.
cp "/lib/$MUSL_LOADER" "$STAGE/lib/"
cp /usr/lib/libgcc_s.so.1 "$STAGE/lib/"

# User-facing launcher: run through the bundled musl loader so the bundle
# works on any Linux, regardless of the host libc.
cat > "$STAGE/bin/nvim" <<EOF
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

BIN_DIR=\$(CDPATH= cd -- "\$(dirname -- "\$0")" && pwd)
ROOT=\$(CDPATH= cd -- "\$BIN_DIR/.." && pwd)

exec "\$ROOT/lib/$MUSL_LOADER" \\
  --library-path "\$ROOT/lib" \\
  "\$BIN_DIR/nvim.real" \\
  "\$@"
EOF

chmod +x "$STAGE/bin/nvim"

tar -C "$STAGE" -czf "$ARCHIVE" .

cd "$DIST_DIR"

sha256sum \
  "nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH.tar.gz" \
  > "nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH.tar.gz.sha256"

echo "$DIST_DIR/nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH.tar.gz"
echo "$DIST_DIR/nvim-portable-linux-$ARCH.tar.gz.sha256"

arguments.content:
name: check

# Watches upstream neovim/neovim for new stable releases. When upstream's
# latest tag differs from this repo's latest release, dispatch the build
# workflow with the tag. Runs hourly; GitHub Actions cron timing is
# best-effort but that is irrelevant at this cadence.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 * * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  actions: write

concurrency:
  group: check
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Compare upstream and local latest tags
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -eu

          UPSTREAM=$(gh api repos/neovim/neovim/releases/latest --jq .tag_name)
          OURS=$(gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/releases/latest" --jq .tag_name \
            || echo "none")

          echo "upstream latest: $UPSTREAM"
          echo "our latest:      $OURS"

          if [ "$UPSTREAM" = "$OURS" ]; then
            echo "Up to date — nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi

          # Sanity: only ever build something that looks like a stable tag.
          case "$UPSTREAM" in
            v*) ;;
            *) echo "Refusing to build unexpected tag: $UPSTREAM" >&2; exit 1 ;;
          esac

          echo "Dispatching build for $UPSTREAM"
          gh workflow run build.yml \
            --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
            -f "tag=$UPSTREAM"

name: build

# Builds portable, musl-bundled Neovim bundles for a given upstream tag and
# publishes them as a release mirroring that tag. Triggered by check.yml when
# a new upstream release appears, or manually with any historical tag to
# backfill a version.

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Upstream neovim tag to build (e.g. v0.11.4)"
        required: true
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: build-${{ inputs.tag }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - arch: x86_64
            runner: ubuntu-24.04
          - arch: aarch64
            runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm

    env:
      ARCH: ${{ matrix.arch }}
      TAG: ${{ inputs.tag }}

    steps:
      - name: Checkout outpost-builds (packaging scripts)
        uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1

      - name: Checkout neovim at ${{ inputs.tag }}
        uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
        with:
          repository: neovim/neovim
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag }}
          path: neovim-src
          # Full history so CMake's `git describe` derives the right version.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Build and package portable Neovim
        run: |
          docker run --rm \
            -v "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE:/work" \
            -w /work/neovim-src \
            -e ARCH="$ARCH" \
            -e SRC_DIR=/work/neovim-src \
            -e DIST_DIR=/work/dist \
            alpine:3.22 \
            sh -c '
              set -eu

              apk add --no-cache \
                build-base \
                cmake \
                coreutils \
                curl \
                gettext-tiny-dev \
                git \
                linux-headers

              make CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

              /work/packaging/package.sh "$ARCH"

              ls -lh /work/dist
            '

      - name: Smoke test portable bundle on Ubuntu
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          rm -rf /tmp/outpost-smoke
          mkdir -p /tmp/outpost-smoke

          tar \
            -xzf "dist/nvim-portable-linux-${ARCH}.tar.gz" \
            -C /tmp/outpost-smoke

          /tmp/outpost-smoke/bin/nvim \
            --clean \
            --headless \
            '+lua vim.treesitter.language.add("lua"); print(vim.env.VIMRUNTIME); print("TREE-SITTER OK")' \
            +qa

      - name: Upload portable bundle
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: nvim-portable-linux-${{ matrix.arch }}
          path: |
            dist/nvim-portable-linux-${{ matrix.arch }}.tar.gz
            dist/nvim-portable-linux-${{ matrix.arch }}.tar.gz.sha256
          if-no-files-found: error

  release:
    needs: build

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    env:
      TAG: ${{ inputs.tag }}

    steps:
      - name: Download build artifacts
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v5
        with:
          pattern: nvim-portable-linux-*
          path: dist
          merge-multiple: true

      - name: Show release assets
        run: ls -lh dist

      - name: Create release (skip if it already exists)
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -eu

          if gh release view "$TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Release $TAG already exists — nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi

          gh release create "$TAG" \
            --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
            --title "$TAG" \
            --notes "Portable musl-bundled Neovim, built from upstream [neovim/neovim](https://github.com/neovim/neovim) at tag \`$TAG\`.

          Assets are single-directory bundles: extract anywhere on a Linux host and run \`bin/nvim\`. No host dependencies (works on glibc and musl systems alike)." \
            dist/*

local M = {}

local REPO = "juniorsundar/outpost-builds"

local tunnels = {}

local function normalize_platform(os_name, arch)
    if os_name ~= "Linux" then
        return nil, "unsupported operating system: " .. os_name
    end

    local arch_map = {
        x86_64 = "x86_64",
        amd64 = "x86_64",

        aarch64 = "aarch64",
        arm64 = "aarch64",
    }

    local normalized_arch = arch_map[arch]

    if not normalized_arch then
        return nil, "unsupported architecture: " .. arch
    end

    return "linux-" .. normalized_arch
end

local function asset_name(platform)
    return "nvim-portable-" .. platform .. ".tar.gz"
end

local function asset_url(tag, asset)
    return string.format("https://github.com/%s/releases/download/%s/%s", REPO, tag, asset)
end

local function latest_tag(callback)
    vim.system({
        "curl",
        "-fsSL",
        "https://api.github.com/repos/" .. REPO .. "/releases/latest",
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(nil, result.stderr or "failed to resolve latest release")
                return
            end

            local ok, decoded = pcall(vim.json.decode, result.stdout)

            if not ok or type(decoded) ~= "table" or not decoded.tag_name then
                callback(nil, "could not parse latest release response")
                return
            end

            callback(decoded.tag_name, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function download(url, path, callback)
    vim.fn.mkdir(vim.fs.dirname(path), "p")

    vim.system({
        "curl",
        "-fL",
        "--output",
        path,
        url,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(nil, result.stderr or "download failed")
                return
            end

            callback(path, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function upload(host, local_path, remote_path, callback)
    vim.system({
        "scp",
        local_path,
        host .. ":" .. remote_path,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "upload failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function verify_sha256(archive_path, checksum_path, callback)
    vim.system({
        "sha256sum",
        "-c",
        checksum_path,
    }, {
        text = true,
        cwd = vim.fs.dirname(archive_path),
    }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or result.stdout or "checksum verification failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, result.stdout)
        end)
    end)
end

-- Resolve a cached archive for the platform/tag, downloading only when the
-- cached copy is missing or fails checksum verification. Multiple remote
-- hosts therefore share a single download.
local function ensure_archive(platform, tag, callback)
    local asset = asset_name(platform)
    local cache_dir = vim.fs.joinpath(vim.fn.stdpath "cache", "outpost", "downloads")

    local archive_path = vim.fs.joinpath(cache_dir, asset)
    local checksum_path = vim.fs.joinpath(cache_dir, asset .. ".sha256")

    local function get_archive(cb)
        download(asset_url(tag, asset), archive_path, function(_, err)
            if err then
                cb(nil, err)
                return
            end

            verify_sha256(archive_path, checksum_path, function(ok, result)
                if not ok then
                    cb(nil, result)
                    return
                end

                cb(archive_path, nil)
            end)
        end)
    end

    download(asset_url(tag, asset .. ".sha256"), checksum_path, function(_, err)
        if err then
            callback(nil, err)
            return
        end

        if not vim.uv.fs_stat(archive_path) then
            get_archive(callback)
            return
        end

        verify_sha256(archive_path, checksum_path, function(ok)
            if ok then
                callback(archive_path, nil)
                return
            end

            get_archive(callback)
        end)
    end)
end

local function remote_version(host, callback)
    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        [[cat "$HOME/.cache/outpost/install/version" 2>/dev/null || exit 1]],
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code == 0 then
                callback(vim.trim(result.stdout))
            else
                callback(nil)
            end
        end)
    end)
end

local function install_remote(host, asset, tag, callback)
    local command = string.format(
        [[
set -eu
INSTALL="$HOME/.cache/outpost/install"
ARCHIVE="$HOME/.cache/outpost/downloads/%s"

rm -rf "$INSTALL/current"
mkdir -p "$INSTALL/current" "$HOME/.cache/outpost/downloads"
tar -xzf "$ARCHIVE" -C "$INSTALL/current"
printf '%%s\n' '%s' > "$INSTALL/version"
]],
        asset,
        tag
    )

    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        command,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "remote install failed")
                return
            end

            callback(true, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function install(host, platform, tag, callback)
    ensure_archive(platform, tag, function(archive, err)
        if not archive then
            callback(false, err)
            return
        end

        vim.system({
            "ssh",
            host,
            "mkdir -p ~/.cache/outpost/downloads",
        }, { text = true }, function(mkdir_result)
            vim.schedule(function()
                if mkdir_result.code ~= 0 then
                    callback(false, mkdir_result.stderr or "remote mkdir failed")
                    return
                end

                local remote_path = "~/.cache/outpost/downloads/" .. vim.fs.basename(archive)

                upload(host, archive, remote_path, function(ok, upload_err)
                    if not ok then
                        callback(false, upload_err)
                        return
                    end

                    install_remote(host, vim.fs.basename(archive), tag, function(ok, install_err)
                        if not ok then
                            callback(false, install_err)
                            return
                        end

                        callback(true, nil)
                    end)
                end)
            end)
        end)
    end)
end

local function start_remote_server(host, callback)
    local command = [[
SOCKET="$HOME/.cache/outpost/run/nvim.sock"
NVIM="$HOME/.cache/outpost/install/current/bin/nvim"

mkdir -p "$HOME/.cache/outpost/run"

if [ -S "$SOCKET" ] && "$NVIM" --server "$SOCKET" --remote-expr '1' >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    exit 0
fi

rm -f "$SOCKET"

nohup "$NVIM" \
  --headless \
  --listen "$SOCKET" \
  >"$HOME/.cache/outpost/run/nvim.log" \
  2>&1 </dev/null &

sleep 1

test -S "$SOCKET"
]]

    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        command,
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(false, result.stderr or "failed to start remote Neovim")
                return
            end

            callback(true, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

local function start_tunnel(host, remote_home, callback)
    local existing = tunnels[host]

    if existing then
        existing.process:kill(15)
        tunnels[host] = nil
    end

    local local_socket = vim.fs.joinpath(
        vim.fn.stdpath("cache"),
        "outpost",
        "run",
        "nvim.sock"
    )

    vim.fn.mkdir(vim.fs.dirname(local_socket), "p")
    vim.fn.delete(local_socket)

    local remote_socket =
        remote_home .. "/.cache/outpost/run/nvim.sock"

    local process = vim.system({
        "ssh",
        "-N",
        "-o",
        "ExitOnForwardFailure=yes",
        "-L",
        local_socket .. ":" .. remote_socket,
        host,
    })

    vim.defer_fn(function()
        if vim.uv.fs_stat(local_socket) then
            tunnels[host] = {
                process = process,
                socket = local_socket,
            }

            callback(true, tunnels[host])
        else
            process:kill(15)
            callback(false, "SSH tunnel did not create local socket")
        end
    end, 1000)
end

local function connect_rpc(socket)
    local channel = vim.fn.sockconnect("pipe", socket, { rpc = true })

    if channel <= 0 then
        return nil, "failed to connect to remote Neovim RPC"
    end

    return channel, nil
end

local function connect_remote(host, remote_home)
    start_remote_server(host, function(started, start_err)
        if not started then
            vim.notify(start_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
            return
        end

        start_tunnel(host, remote_home, function(ok, tunnel)
            if not ok then
                vim.notify(tunnel, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            local channel, rpc_err = connect_rpc(tunnel.socket)

            if not channel then
                vim.notify(rpc_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            local version = vim.rpcrequest(
                channel,
                "nvim_exec_lua",
                [[
                    local v = vim.version()
                    return string.format(
                        "%d.%d.%d%s",
                        v.major,
                        v.minor,
                        v.patch,
                        v.prerelease and "-dev" or ""
                    )
                ]],
                {}
            )

            vim.notify("remote Neovim: " .. version)
        end)
    end)
end

local function resolve_remote(host, callback)
    vim.system({
        "ssh",
        host,
        [[printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n' "$(uname -s)" "$(uname -m)" "$HOME"]],
    }, { text = true }, function(result)
        vim.schedule(function()
            if result.code ~= 0 then
                callback(nil, result.stderr or "ssh probe failed")
                return
            end

            local lines = vim.split(vim.trim(result.stdout), "\n")
            local remote_home = lines[3]

            local platform, err = normalize_platform(lines[1], lines[2])

            if not platform then
                callback(nil, err)
                return
            end

            callback({
                platform = platform,
                home = remote_home,
            }, nil)
        end)
    end)
end

function M.probe(host)
    resolve_remote(host, function(remote, err)
        if not remote then
            vim.notify(err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
            return
        end

        latest_tag(function(tag, tag_err)
            if not tag then
                vim.notify(tag_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            remote_version(host, function(installed)
                if installed == tag then
                    connect_remote(host, remote.home)
                    return
                end

                if installed then
                    vim.notify(
                        string.format(
                            "outpost: update available (%s -> %s). Run :OutpostUpdate %s",
                            installed,
                            tag,
                            host
                        ),
                        vim.log.levels.WARN
                    )
                    return
                end

                vim.notify("outpost: installing Neovim " .. tag .. " on " .. host)
                install(host, remote.platform, tag, function(ok, install_err)
                    if not ok then
                        vim.notify(install_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                        return
                    end

                    connect_remote(host, remote.home)
                end)
            end)
        end)
    end)
end

function M.update(host)
    resolve_remote(host, function(remote, err)
        if not remote then
            vim.notify(err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
            return
        end

        latest_tag(function(tag, tag_err)
            if not tag then
                vim.notify(tag_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                return
            end

            remote_version(host, function(installed)
                if installed == tag then
                    vim.notify("outpost: " .. host .. " already on " .. tag)
                    connect_remote(host, remote.home)
                    return
                end

                if installed then
                    vim.notify(string.format("outpost: updating %s (%s -> %s)", host, installed, tag))
                else
                    vim.notify("outpost: installing Neovim " .. tag .. " on " .. host)
                end

                install(host, remote.platform, tag, function(ok, install_err)
                    if not ok then
                        vim.notify(install_err, vim.log.levels.ERROR)
                        return
                    end

                    connect_remote(host, remote.home)
                end)
            end)
        end)
    end)
end

function M.setup()
    local function command_opts()
        return {
            nargs = 1,
        }
    end

    vim.api.nvim_create_user_command("Outpost", function(opts)
        M.probe(opts.args)
    end, command_opts())

    vim.api.nvim_create_user_command("OutpostUpdate", function(opts)
        M.update(opts.args)
    end, command_opts())
end

return M

Good question to ask now — the plumbing (provision, tunnel, connect) is done, but the plugin doesn't yet let you *edit anything*. Let me lay out the feature map, because the order matters: everything else hangs off the UI-attach architecture decision.

## The architecture insight that drives everything

You already chose the right model (it's exactly what vscode-server does, adapted to Neovim's client/server design):

- **UI runs locally, everything else runs remotely.** Neovim has this natively: `nvim --server <tunneled-socket> --remote-ui` attaches a local terminal UI to the remote instance. Once that works, buffers, file explorers, telescope, LSP, and `:terminal` (remote shell!) all operate on remote files *for free*, with zero extra code.
- **The consequence:** the config and plugins must live on the *remote* — that's the nvim process that runs them. Your sync idea isn't a nice-to-have; it's structurally required. The remote server currently boots with stock defaults, so there's nothing to attach *to* that feels like your setup.

## Minimal feature ladder

**1. UI attach — the one thing to get out of the way first.** `:Outpost <host>` should end with you *in* the remote instance, not a notification with a version string. Design question embedded: `--remote-ui` is a startup flag, so the local instance that runs `:Outpost` can't attach itself mid-flight. Cleanest UX is a launcher-style command (`nvim --server <sock> --remote-ui`) spawned as a subprocess in a `:terminal` buffer, or a companion command that re-execs. Everything else layers on this.

**2. Project targeting.** `:Outpost host:~/code/project` (vscode's "Open Folder" equivalent) — set the remote cwd at attach time via `nvim_set_current_dir`. Plus a way to list/reconnect to running remote sessions, since a headless server is a *persistent* session: detach by killing the tunnel, reattach later. This is your edge over vscode — the session survives the disconnect.

**3. Config + plugin sync** (your consideration — here's what it actually involves):
- **rsync over the existing ssh path** is the right primitive for config: fast, incremental, and git isn't guaranteed on the remote host beyond our bundle (though we could ship git in the bundle later, since the portable tarball is ours to shape).
- **Plugins**: let lazy.nvim bootstrap on the remote (clone from GitHub there) rather than rsyncing thousands of files — sync only your config, then `Lazy sync` on the remote.
- **The trap: treesitter parsers are arch-specific binaries.** You can't rsync compiled `.so` parsers, and our portable bundle ships *no compiler*. Options: (a) bundle `zig cc`/musl-gcc in the portable bundle so nvim-treesitter can build parsers remotely, (b) ship prebuilt parsers from outpost-builds, or (c) detect a system compiler. This is the single hardest dependency in the whole project — decide it consciously.
- **LSP servers** (Mason): mostly need node on the remote — detect, warn, or forward. Out of MVP scope; just surface a health check.

**4. Clipboard sync — the subtle must-solve.** The remote nvim can't see your local clipboard; yank/paste feels broken immediately. OSC52 is the standard answer (works through the tunnel because the UI is local) — configure the remote's clipboard provider to OSC52. Small, but without it the experience feels fundamentally broken.

**5. Session lifecycle & connection hygiene:**
- Tunnel keepalive/auto-reconnect (ssh dies on network blips; currently the tunnel process is fire-and-forget).
- `:OutpostStop <host>` to tear down the remote server.
- **ssh ControlMaster multiplexing** — right now *every step* (probe, mkdir, scp, install, server-start) opens a fresh ssh connection, each paying full auth + TCP RTT. One master connection for a host turns 6 connection setups into 1. Cheap change, big perceived-speed win.

**"What else" — later tiers:**

| Feature | Why | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| `:OutpostForward <port>` | DAP debugging, preview servers — vscode's port forwarding | small, reuse tunnel code |
| Env/credential forwarding | `ssh-agent` forwarding so git push works remotely | mostly docs/flags |
| Host aliases & per-project hosts | `.outpost` marker file, completion for `:Outpost` | small |
| Version parity check | local vs outpost-builds nvim API drift breaking shared config | small |
| Health check command | audits remote: compilers, node, git, disk | small |

My recommendation for sequencing: **UI attach first** (it's the product), then **cwd targeting**, then **ssh multiplexing** (2-line change, unblocks fast iteration), then take on **config sync + treesitter** as the second big slice since that's where the real design decisions are.

Right — let's design the behavior contract before writing a line of code. Here's my proposed architecture for the attach feature and the session model it implies, with the decision points called out.

## The user-visible story (what `:Outpost` should *mean*)

```
:Outpost devbox:~/code/neovim
```

1. **Resolve** — is there a session for `devbox` + `~/code/neovim`? (see session model below)
2. **Provision if needed** — install/verify the portable nvim, sync config if stale (later slice), ensure a headless server is running *with that directory as its cwd*.
3. **Tunnel** — forward the session's socket locally.
4. **Attach** — you are now editing remote files with your own config, LSP running on the remote, `:terminal` gives you a remote shell. Killing the local attach client (or closing nvim) **does not kill the session** — the headless server persists on the remote, buffers and all.
5. **Reattach** — running the same command later reconnects to the *existing* session state. This persistence is outpost's identity: it's a *project workspace that lives on the remote*, not a one-off edit.

## Session model: (host, project path) — not just host

This is the architectural consequence of "project-level work." I propose:

- **A session is identified by `(host, abspath)`.** Each session gets its own remote server: `~/.cache/outpost/run/<session-id>/nvim.sock` where `session-id` is a short hash of the path (or the path's basename, dedup'd).
- **One session = one nvim process = one UI client max.** `--remote-ui` allows exactly one attached UI, so attach must check `nvim_list_uis()` over RPC first and refuse (with a clear message) if another client is already attached.
- **Current code has a latent bug this fixes**: the local tunnel socket is a fixed path (`stdpath/cache)/outpost/run/nvim.sock`), so two concurrent hosts collide. Per-session local sockets fix that for free.
- Consequence: switching projects = `:Outpost host:~/code/other` creates/attaches a *different* session, while the first one keeps running. `:cd` on an attached session is just movement within that project — session identity is set at creation.
- `:OutpostList` shows known sessions from a **local registry** (stdpath data): host, path, remote session id, last-attached time — powers completion too (`:Outpost devbox:<Tab>` offers known projects).

## Lifecycle state machine

```
   :Outpost h:p                       detach (close client/tunnel)
┌─────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐
│ absent                  │        │              ▼
└──► provisioning ──► running ◄──────────────── running (detached)
                        │   ▲                         │
                        │   └── reattach ◄── :Outpost h:p (same session)
                        │
                        │ host reboot / kill
                        ▼
                      stopped ──► :Outpost h:p re-provisions & starts fresh
```

- Attach always *reconciles*: probe → is server alive? socket healthy? correct cwd? If the remote rebooted, restart it (fresh state — document that state loss happens only on explicit stop or remote reboot).
- `:OutpostStop [h:p]` tears down the remote server. Detach ≠ stop.
- Tunnel needs **supervision**: currently the ssh process is fire-and-forget. An attached client whose tunnel dies should notice and offer reconnect (and the registry lets us kill orphaned tunnels by PID).

## The one genuinely hard UX decision: what attaches?

`--remote-ui` is a startup flag — a *running* nvim can't attach itself. Three viable shapes:

- **A. Nested client in `:terminal`**: `:Outpost` provisions, then spawns `nvim --server <sock> --remote-ui` in a terminal buffer of the current instance. Works today, some nesting friction (nested esc, colors, one pane inside your nvim). This is what remote-nvim.nvim does.
- **B. Shell launcher as the primary UX**: `outpost devbox:~/code/neovim` in your terminal runs a small headless bootstrap (same Lua module, `--headless`) that provisions, then `exec`s the attaching nvim *as the foreground process*. Full-screen, zero nesting — the cleanest daily-driver experience. More machinery (a CLI shim, bootstrap mode in the module).
- **C. Both**: `:Outpost` in nvim does A; the same plumbing gives you B for free. B is honestly where a project-level tool wants to end up — vscode-server's entry point is also "a fresh window," not a pane inside an existing editor.

## Prerequisites the design must acknowledge (gates, not blockers)

- **v1 attach works against stock remote config.** We validate attach with a bare `--clean` server first, because sync is a separate slice with its own hard problems (treesitter parsers are arch-specific binaries and the bundle has no compiler; git isn't in the bundle but config bootstrap likely needs it → **outpost-builds v2 bundle contents** is a coupled decision: ship `git` — and eventually a musl compiler — inside the portable tarball?).
- **Attach UX details that make or break it**: clipboard must use OSC52 on the remote (else yank/paste feels broken); ssh ControlMaster multiplexing so provisioning isn't 6 sequential auth round-trips; compression (`ssh -C`) for the chatty UI protocol on high-latency links.
- **Version parity**: the local attaching client and the remote server should be same-ish versions; we can surface a warning on mismatch via the RPC handshake we already do.

## Command surface (proposed, for the doc)

| Command | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `:Outpost <host>[:<path>]` | Reconcile + attach (create session if absent) |
| `:OutpostList` | Registry browser: sessions, states, attach/stop actions |
| `:OutpostStop [host[:path]]` | Stop remote server(s); no arg = current/interactive |
| `:OutpostUpdate <host>` | Existing behavior (re-pins portable nvim) |
| `:OutpostRemove <host>` | Uninstall the portable install from remote (later) |

Completion: hosts from `~/.ssh/config` + known sessions from the registry.

2. Registry lookup by hash. If a session exists and the remote server is healthy (probe `--remote-expr` on the session socket, like today's logic), **skip to 5** — launch is idempotent.
3. Otherwise provision: ensure portable install on host (existing logic), start headless server with **cwd = the project path**, socket at `~/.cache/outpost/run/<hash>/nvim.sock` on the remote.
4. Register `{hash, host, path, created}` in the local registry (`stdpath(data)/outpost/registry.json`).
5. **Print the attach command** — a generated, self-contained launcher script:
   ```
   ~/.cache/nvim/outpost/attach/<hash>.sh
   ```
   The script opens its own `ssh -L` tunnel to the session socket, runs `nvim --server <local-sock> --remote-ui` in the foreground, and tears down its tunnel on exit. The plugin's current `start_tunnel`/`tunnels` table moves *into this script* — the plugin itself never holds a tunnel again.

- For every registry entry, ssh-probe (in parallel, with timeout): is the session server alive?

My proposal: entries where ssh **succeeds but no server** = dead → removed from registry; entries where **ssh itself fails** = flagged `unreachable` and kept (or purged with `:Outpost! list`). Never auto-destroy anything on the remote during GC — removal is registry-local only.

- Note the blast radius: `stop` kills one *session*; the host-wide portable install stays (that's `update` territory).

- Updates the host-wide `install/current`; running sessions keep their already-loaded binary (Linux inode semantics) and pick up the new one on next launch.

- The wording "only from current machine" settles the earlier git-bootstrap-vs-rsync question: **rsync is the source of truth** (no lazy.nvim bootstrap on the remote). Simple, deterministic, works on hosts without git.

- `:Outpost stop <Tab>` → live hashes from `list` logic

# Outpost — Design

Outpost is a vscode-server-like remote development layer for Neovim:
provision a portable, musl-bundled Neovim on a remote host, run a persistent
headless project session there, and attach a local `--remote-ui` client to it
from a separate terminal.

## Core model

- **Outpost is a control plane.** The plugin runs inside a *local* nvim and
  manages remote sessions. It does not own tunnels or attached clients.
- **Sessions are project-scoped**, identified by `(user@host, absolute path)`.
  Each session is one headless remote nvim server with the project directory
  as its cwd and its own socket: `~/.cache/outpost/run/<hash>/nvim.sock`.
- **Attach is external and self-contained.** The plugin hands the user a
  launcher script; the script owns its tunnel + attaching client lifecycle and
  works independently of the nvim that launched it.
- **Sessions persist across attaches.** Detaching (closing the attaching
  terminal) leaves the remote server running. Only `stop` (or the remote host
  dying) destroys session state.
- **One UI client per session.** `--remote-ui` allows a single attached UI;
  launch must refuse (with a clear warning) when `nvim_list_uis()` shows one
  already attached.

## Session identity

- `hash = sha256(user@host + ":" + abspath)[:6]` (6 hex chars).
- Local registry: `stdpath("data")/outpost/registry.json` —
  `{hash, user@host, path, created_at, last_used_at}`.
- Host-wide portable install (shared by all sessions on that host):
  `~/.cache/outpost/install/current`, version pinned in
  `~/.cache/outpost/install/version`.

## Command surface

Single command, subcommand dispatch: `:Outpost <subcommand> [args]`
(`:Outpost! <subcommand>` = no-confirmation variant where applicable).

### `:Outpost launch user@host:/abs/path`

1. Resolve the session hash; check the registry.
2. If a healthy session already exists for it (socket probe via
   `--remote-expr`), skip to 5 — launch is idempotent.
3. Otherwise provision: ensure the portable install (download from
   `outpost-builds` latest release, checksum, scp, extract — current logic),
   then start a headless server with cwd = the project path.
4. Register the session in the local registry.
5. Print the attach command: a generated launcher at
   `<stdpath cache>/outpost/attach/<hash>.sh`, which opens its own `ssh -L`
   tunnel to the session socket, runs `nvim --server <local-sock> --remote-ui`
   in the foreground, and tears its tunnel down on exit.

Warn if another UI client is already attached to the session.

### `:Outpost list`

- ssh-probe every registry entry (parallel, timeout-bounded).
- Show: hash · host · path · state (`live` / `dead` / `unreachable`).
- Garbage collection: remove *dead* entries (ssh reachable, but no server) —
  registry-local removal only, never touching the remote. Entries where ssh
  itself fails are `unreachable`: kept and flagged by default; purged with
  `:Outpost! list`.

### `:Outpost stop <hash>`

- Kill the remote session server, remove its `run/<hash>/` dir, drop the
  registry entry. Confirmation unless banged.
- Scope: kills one *session*. The host-wide portable install is untouched
  (see `update`).

### `:Outpost update user@host`

- Re-resolve the latest release from `outpost-builds`, install to the host.
  Running sessions keep their loaded binary and pick the new one up on next
  launch.

### `:Outpost sync user@host`

- rsync plugins + runtime files, local machine → remote (local is the source
  of truth; no git bootstrap on the remote).
- Scope/exclusions TBD (config dir, plugin dirs; exclude `.git`?, compiled
  artifacts?). Known constraint: treesitter parsers are arch-specific — must
  be excluded on arch mismatch and rebuilt (requires a compiler on the
  remote; open question whether outpost-builds bundles one).

## Completion

- `:Outpost <Tab>` → subcommands
- `:Outpost launch <Tab>` → hosts from `~/.ssh/config`, then `host:path`
  combos from the registry
- `:Outpost stop <Tab>` → live session hashes
- `:Outpost sync|update <Tab>` → registry + ssh-config hosts

## Distribution

- Portable Neovim builds: https://github.com/juniorsundar/outpost-builds
  (hourly cron mirrors upstream stable releases; assets
  `nvim-portable-linux-{x86_64,aarch64}.tar.gz`).
- Client resolves `releases/latest` dynamically; no pinned tags in the plugin.

## Open questions

1. GC policy for ssh-unreachable hosts: keep-and-flag (current decision) vs
   aggressive purge.
2. `launch` with no path: error (path required — project-level tool) vs
   default `~`.
3. Where the attach command is presented: `:messages` vs floating buffer with
   automatic `+` clipboard yank.
4. outpost-builds bundle v2 contents: ship `git`? a musl compiler (for
   treesitter parser builds)? node (for LSP)?
5. Version parity warning between the attaching local client and the remote
   server (RPC handshake already queries the remote version).

Alright — you asked to be grilled. Here's the interrogation. Some of these I think should overturn decisions in the design doc; I'll say which and why. Answer what you can; push back where I'm wrong.

---

**1. Why is a hash the user-facing identity at all? ★**

You said *"Outpost list will show a hash that can be called with Outpost stop"*. That's machine identity leaking into the UX. Six opaque characters mean: you can't tell two outposts apart in `list` without reading the host/path anyway, and `stop ab12cd` requires you to first run `list`, then transcribe. So who is the hash *for*? If it's for the remote dir naming and registry key — fine, keep it internal. But for the user, `stop devbox:~/code/neovim` or an interactive `list` that lets you hit `d` on a row does the same job with zero memorization. What does the hash buy the *user* that host:path doesn't?

**2. The local registry is a second source of truth. That's a bug factory. ★**

The design says `list` iterates the *local registry*. But the remote's `~/.cache/outpost/run/` *is* the ground truth — it survives registry deletion, local machine switches (you on a laptop *and* a desktop? two registries, each half-blind), or a `~/.cache` wipe. Concretely: you attach from your laptop via a hand-written command, then run `list` from your desktop — the session exists on the remote, is invisible in your registry. What should happen? My push: **registry is only a cache/enrichment layer; `list` scans the remote `run/` dir via ssh and reconciles the registry to it** (adopt unknown sessions, drop dead ones). Registry "disagreement" can't occur because one side is authoritative. Do you accept demoting the registry, or do you want it authoritative and accept the blind spots?

**3. Path canonicalization — your hash is broken by a trailing slash. ★**

`:Outpost launch user@host:/home/user/Documents/Project` and `:Outpost launch user@host:/home/user/Documents/Project/` and `~/Documents/Project` and `~/code/../code/Project` are **four different hashes for the same session**. Same for symlinks: `/home/user/Documents/Project` vs `/mnt/data/Project` where one symlinks the other — two servers, one directory, and only one can be right about cwd. My push: resolve the path with `realpath` *on the remote* before hashing, always. That also gives you "same project, two users" disambiguation for free (`user@` is part of the key — good, keep that). Objection?

**4. What does the second attacher see? ★**

You decided: refuse with a warning if a UI is already attached. Play the scenario: you attached from the office, ssh dropped (network blip), your terminal died, the *remote* still thinks the UI is attached (or does it? — does nvim notice a dead RPC client? It does, but there's a timeout window). Now you're blocked out of your own session for refusing reasons that are nobody's fault. Alternatives: **takeover** — detach the stale UI via `nvim_ui_detach` then attach fresh (vscode's behavior: old window goes dead, new one wins); or takeover-with-grace-period. Which do you want, and does "refuse" survive this scenario in your head?

**5. Which nvim runs the attach script?**

The generated script presumably runs `nvim --server ... --remote-ui` — *which* nvim? `PATH` nvim? The version that launched it (`vim.vim.progpath`)? Why does this matter: the attaching client is a TUI renderer for the remote's API; a local 0.9 client against a remote 0.12 server speaks an older RPC dialect and can misrender or crash. If the remote runs `v0.12.5` from outpost-builds, your *local* nvim is whatever your distro/nix gave you — possibly older. Should the attach script pin the same `outpost-builds` binary *locally* (download once, cache) so client and server versions match exactly? That's the truly vscode-server-shaped answer: both ends from the same artifact store. Cost: first-attach downloads 12MB locally. Yes or no?

**6. Where's ControlMaster in the doc?**

I raised it in the feature ladder; the design doc dropped it. Count the ssh handshakes in one cold `launch`: probe platform → version check → mkdir → scp (new connection!) → install extract → server start → UI check. Seven sequential auth round-trips, each potentially 1–3s. With ControlMaster it's one handshake and the rest are milliseconds over the mux. This isn't an optimization nicety, it's the difference between `launch` feeling instant and feeling sluggish. Should the plugin just always pass `-o ControlMaster=auto -o ControlPath=... -o ControlPersist=10m` on every invocation? Any reason you'd refuse (shared CI hosts where stale mux sockets rot)?

**7. Socket permissions — is the remote host shared?**

`--listen` sockets get default-ish permissions. If the remote box is shared (university server, VPS with other users), anyone who can access `~/.cache/outpost/run/<hash>/nvim.sock` can attach — and an attached UI is *full code execution as you*. Single-user boxes: don't care. Multi-user boxes: `chmod 700` on the run dir + socket, maybe verify at launch and warn. Do your target hosts have other users, ever?

**8. `sync` — define "runtime files" or it'll be wrong. ★**

You said *"sync plugins and runtime files only from current machine"*. Unpack that for me, because it hides four decisions:

- **Which dirs?** `stdpath('config')` (your whole dotfiles nvim config — includes the outpost submodule itself, fine) and the lazy.nvim plugin tree (`stdpath('data')/lazy`)? Or the plugin tree derived from `rtp`?
- **Plugin `.git` dirs: keep or strip?** Keep → lazy.nvim is satisfied, lockfile works, sync is bigger. Strip → smaller sync, lazy re-clones on remote first boot (needs git on remote — currently absent from the bundle).
- **Compiled parsers**: excluded on arch mismatch *and then what*? Rebuild needs a compiler that doesn't exist on the remote. So either outpost-builds ships a musl gcc, or outpost-builds ships *prebuilt parsers per arch* (they can be built in the same CI matrix — honestly cleaner), or you accept no treesitter remotely. This is the single decision the whole sync slice rotates on.
- **Config divergence**: your config will need remote-only tweaks (OSC52 clipboard, maybe disabling local-only plugins, different colorscheme for slow links?). An overlay file (`outpost.remote.lua` synced *in addition* and applied at startup)? Or does the remote get the config verbatim and you refactor config to branch on `vim.g.outpost_remote`? The second keeps one source of truth — I'd push for that.

Answer even loosely — this becomes the sync spec.

**9. What kills the leftover sockets?**

Attach script cleans its tunnel on exit — but only on *graceful* exit. SIGKILL'd terminal, crashed ssh, rebooted laptop: stale local socket files and possibly zombie `ssh -L` processes accumulate. Who reaps? Options: attach script traps EXIT/TERM (best effort, kills won't trap), or `launch` sweeps stale sockets for the target session before printing (ssh-free, local-only, cheap). Also: stale *mux* sockets from #6. Is "best effort + sweep on next launch" good enough for you?

**10. Is `launch` even the right name?**

Small, but you'll type it for years: `launch` *implies* starting something new, yet the command's primary behavior on re-run is "already exists → print me the attach command." Candidates: `open` (vscode verb, but overloaded), `connect`, `up` (docker compose verb — "bring it up or reuse it"), or keep `launch`. Also: what's the *command you run in the other terminal* — is it acceptable UX that attaching requires copy-pasting a path, or should the plugin also install a stable global shim (e.g., `~/.local/bin/outpost-attach <hash>` that self-provisions *headlessly* and execs, so eventually `outpost devbox:~/proj` works from a bare shell with zero nvim running)? Is that shim the real end-state and the `:Outpost` command just the bootstrap?

---

The starred ones (1, 2, 3, 4, 8) are the points where I believe the current design doc is actually *wrong or underspecified* in a way that will bite during implementation — I'd settle those before anything else. The rest are hardening. Fire away.

Now to the real question — **what is an outpost?** Your own usage has been oscillating, and that's exactly the ambiguity to kill:

- "Outpost stop hash to destroy an **outpost**" → an outpost sounds like a *session*
- "Outpost update user@host will update the **outpost** neovim version" → an outpost sounds like a *host installation*

These are different entities with different lifecycles, and conflating them will produce mushy commands. Here's the three-tier model I propose — with names, since you asked for vocabulary that survives into future conversations:

## The entity model

```
BASE                          OUTPOST                     PROJECT
(local machine)               (per remote host)            (per directory)
┌──────────────────┐    ssh   ┌────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│ your config      │ ───────► │ ~/.cache/outpost/       │  │ ~/code/foo   │
│ your plugins     │  sync    │   install/  (portable)  │  │ git repo,    │
│ outpost.nvim     │          │   run/<id>/ (sessions)  │  │ NOT ours     │
│ attach client    │◄───────► │                         │  └──────────────┘
└──────────────────┘  tunnel │      SESSIONS           │
                              │   nvim server, cwd =    │
                              │   project dir, state     │
                              └────────────────────────┘
```

- **Base** — your local machine. Owns: credentials, the config/plugin *source of truth*, the plugin itself (control plane), and the attaching clients. *(Name candidates if "base" doesn't land: `homeport`, `citadel`, `haven` — I'd pick `base` for brevity in docs and code identifiers.)*
- **Outpost** — the *installation* on one remote host: the portable nvim, the synced config/plugins, all session sockets. Shared across every project on that host. Disposable by design. `update` and `sync` act at this scope.
- **Session** — one headless nvim server *inside* an outpost, bound to one project directory. Owns the editing state: buffers, windows, LSP, terminals. `launch`, `stop`, `list` act at this scope. No cute name — it maps 1:1 onto nvim's own vocabulary.
- **Project** — the directory itself. Explicitly *not owned* by anyone here: it's your data, pre-existing. The outpost merely points at it. Corollary: `stop`/remove can never touch project files.

## Scope of authority (the rules)

1. **The base is the only authority.** Outposts and sessions never act autonomously — no self-update, no cron, no systemd units on the remote. Everything happens because a base commanded it, or because the user is acting *through* an attached session (`:terminal`, tests, git — that's you wielding the session, not the session having agency).
2. **Material flows one way.** Config and plugins sync base → outpost, never back. The outpost is never a source of truth for anything but *session state*.
3. **Outposts are cattle.** An outpost is reproducible from `(upstream release + base sync)`. Destroying one loses nothing but session state.
4. **Session state is the one non-reproducible thing — and we declare it lossy.** Remote reboot, `stop`, oom-kill: session state dies and that's *by policy*, not a bug. (Detach ≠ death, but reboot does. This should be printed in the docs in bold.)
5. **Credentials are forwarded, never stored.** ssh-agent forwarding at attach time so git push works *from* the session; no keys ever land on the outpost.
6. **Discovery scans the remote, not the registry.** This dissolves grilling point #2: the outpost's `run/` directory is ground truth for what sessions exist; the local registry is a cache for completion speed and enrichment, reconciled on every `list`. Two local machines → both converge on reality by scanning.

Rule 6 is the one that overturns a previous decision (registry-first `list`), and rules 3–4 give us clean answers to grilling #9 (nothing needs reaping carefully — stale stuff is garbage by definition) and simplify `stop` (no "what if I lose something" anxiety: the answer is "session state, by design").

Without canonicalization that's two sessions, two servers, two sockets — and both *editing the same files simultaneously*, which is a genuine correctness problem, not a UX nit (two nvim instances, one working tree, no swapfile coordination). With it, same session, reconnect. The only wrinkle is #12: `realpath` needs the dir to exist, which forces the doesn't-exist decision first. My proposed chain: **resolve `~` → `realpath` on remote → if missing, offer mkdir → hash the canonical path**. Anything you want different, or do I write it into the spec as settled?

**14. Takeover — one correction to my own claim.**

I said `nvim_ui_detach` — wrong tool, that detaches *your own channel's* UI. The correct mechanism is `chanclose(<id>)` on the attached UI's channel (from `nvim_list_uis()`/`nvim_list_chans()` over the control-plane RPC), which kills the stale client and frees the UI slot. Also worth noting in your favor of takeover: when your ssh connection drops, the *remote* nvim often notices the socket close and detaches the dead client on its own — the refusal scenario is real but narrower than I painted it: it's mostly "I closed my attach terminal but the process lingers" and "reconnecting during nvim's own grace window." So the design becomes: **`up` checks UIs; if one is attached and its channel is responsive, offer takeover (chanclose + hand out command); if unresponsive, takeover silently.** Do you accept takeover as the rule, or do you want refusal when a live UI is demonstrably present?

**15. Sync — the parser question deserves its own fight, because "outpost-builds ships prebuilt parsers" was too glib. ★**

My earlier suggestion has a hole: your CI can't know which parsers your config's `ensure_installed` wants, so "prebuilt parsers in the bundle" means either shipping all ~60 (bloat for everyone, stale relative to your config's needs) or a manifest you maintain (toil). The alternative I now think is better: **sync works differently depending on arch parity** —

- **Arch match** (e.g. your x86_64 base → x86_64 outpost): rsync the plugin tree *including compiled `parser/*.so`* — they just work, zero compiler needed on the remote.
- **Arch mismatch** (x86_64 base → aarch64 outpost): exclude compiled parsers, and you need a compiler on the remote *only in this case*. Ship `zig` (single self-contained ~45MB binary, `nvim-treesitter` supports `CC='zig cc'`) as an *optional* outpost-builds asset — `sync` downloads it on the remote only when arches mismatch and parsers need rebuilding.

Most users live in the arch-match case and never see a compiler at all. Is mismatch support even something you need (are your real outposts mixed-arch? your CI builds both — so maybe yes)? Or do we ship v1 as arch-match-only, warn on mismatch, and defer zig?
